model_reported.summary: Proposed a three-accumulator scalar scan to test an intermediate unroll factor against the measured two- and four-accumulator candidates.

model_reported.summary: Used the supplied frozen target facts: AMD EPYC 9654, GCC 14.2, x86_64, and one core; no environment change is proposed.

model_reported.name: consulter-documentation-technique
model_reported.summary: This change uses ordinary scalar C++ control flow and no target-specific API or instruction, so documentation was not needed.

model_reported.name: evaluer-performances
model_reported.summary: Compared the supplied aggregate timings and correctness outcomes without inferring per-pattern performance or claiming an unmeasured speedup.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use three accumulators as a contrasting intermediate unroll factor; do not infer per-pattern behavior from aggregate timings.
memory_lessons.claim: The valid two-accumulator program measured 2.260 microseconds on average, the valid four-accumulator program 2.813 microseconds, and the valid baseline 4.463 microseconds. These aggregate measurements rank the tested programs but do not establish per-pattern effects or the cause.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this three-accumulator candidate after correctness validation and compare its aggregate and available random/decreasing-input results under the same protocol.

proposal.hypothesis: A three-accumulator scalar scan may retain useful independent dependency chains while reducing per-accumulator and fold overhead relative to the selected four-accumulator parent. The measured two-accumulator candidate is faster in aggregate than four, so no monotonic benefit from adding accumulators is assumed; this intermediate factor tests that tradeoff on random and decreasing inputs after correctness checks.

retained: Replaced the four-way scalar scan with three independent minimum-value and earliest-index accumulators processing indices in modulo-three lanes.
Folded accumulator results by signed minimum value with lowest-index tie-breaking, then handled any remainder scalarly.
Retained explicit small-size and nonpositive-size handling; used neither explicit SIMD nor parallel workers.
